extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on creating, distributing, and placing public relations messages (including press releases, VNRs, PSAs) across media channels — wire services, syndicates, magazines, radio, television, cable, and new/digital media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of commercial wire services
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations wire services charge clients to electronically transmit text, photographs, audio and video news releases and regulatory postings to the media and other organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wire services offer fast, simultaneous transmission to many media outlets and are used for major corporate developments, earnings reports, obituaries, invitations to news conferences, and emergencies such as product recalls. Clients pay fees based on distribution ordered; media receive the services at no charge. Wire services also sell monitoring and measurement services to provide metrics on dissemination, placements, and potential audience size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syndicates for features, photos, and columns
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature, photo, and specialized news syndicates place material widely and economically and increase acceptability of material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement with a syndicate ensures wide distribution (e.g., United Feature Syndicate distributes columns, commentaries, cartoons, comic strips) and syndicates charge fees based on each medium's circulation or audience size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature services sponsored by clients (free-to-media model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some feature services supply newspapers and periodicals with material without charge; sponsoring clients pay the bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples such as North American Precis Syndicate (NAPS) distribute consumer news and information and provide video news releases, B-roll, animated stills, and radio spots to thousands of outlets. Practitioners can leverage these services to reach many publications and broadcasters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target magazines for narrowly defined audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Magazines and specialized publications provide channels to reach audiences who share specific interests and enable targeted messaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should study magazines’ topics, styles, policies, trends, and formats and then target news and features to specific magazines rather than submitting unsolicited material. Many magazines have online editions; some audiences still prefer print.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand magazines' lead times and competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Magazine publicity placement requires awareness of long lead times and stiff competition for space from editors, staff writers, frequent contributors, and freelancers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many practitioners fail because they do not account for lead time or competitive pressures. Submit story outlines or feature suggestions on a tip/query basis and be prepared to work cooperatively with magazine staff or freelance writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work with freelance writers and meet their story criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Freelance writers who regularly sell to national magazines look for stories with (1) national importance or significance; (2) elements of struggle, conflict, contest, or drama; and (3) anecdotal enrichment and entertainment value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a story meets these qualities, give it to a known freelancer who can develop it for the magazine; the practitioner benefits from the publicity placement while the freelancer is paid by the magazine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use magazines for durable, in-depth treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Magazines provide more durable information than newspapers and allow readers to read, reread, discuss, and debate topics in depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magazines influence opinion leaders, shape preferences and professional standards, and remain important even in online formats—many readers still want printed copies. Use magazines for topics requiring depth and longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage radio's mobile reach and intimate tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Radio is a mobile, person-to-person medium that reaches listeners in many daily contexts and conveys a direct, personal touch through the spoken word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Radio listening remains high; radio reaches people in cars, at home, and online. Use radio to reach specific audiences and exploit its conversational nature (e.g., call-in shows) for discussion and public debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribute radio news releases and audio feeds; localize content
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations practitioners use radio news releases and audio feeds sent to stations through networks; distribution is over the Internet or telephone lines to target stations by region and format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To increase local station airings, supply interviews or sound bites that stations can localize. Examples include CNN Podcasts and other audio distribution services that deliver news cutaways and updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use call-in talk shows and telephone interviews strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Call-in talk shows and telephone interviews provide forums for public debate and can set the public agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talk shows often capitalize on local conflict and sensational topics; they have an appetite for guests with a message. Use these formats when the story matches the show's orientation and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public service announcement (PSA) format and station standards
rubrics_metrics.description: PSAs typically come in 10-second, 30-second, or 60-second lengths and promote programs and services of government and voluntary agencies for which no payment is made to the station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stations set their own standards and most use well-prepared PSAs. Free public service time is often non-prime but still valuable; nonprofit groups can access some prime time depending on station community relations policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television's strengths and time/format limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Television combines multiple modes (printed word, spoken word, video, music, animation) making it powerful for storytelling, but time limits force compression and selection of the most 'effective bit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even major stories receive limited time (e.g., network evening news), which can oversimplify or distort complex issues. Plan television messages to fit short formats and emphasize vivid, compelling moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitching television producers and ethical issues with VNRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners pitch story ideas to TV producers and increasingly provide video in the form of video news releases (VNRs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics argue it is unethical to use VNRs in newscasts without telling viewers that an outside source provided the video; RTDNA warns about this practice. Most stations require disclosure or clear labeling when using VNR content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Satellite Media Tours (SMTs) under appropriate conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: SMTs enable distributed interviews via satellite, replacing time-consuming city hopping for fast, broad coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SMTs work best when local stations cannot produce the same story, when the story fits morning programming before being bumped by breaking news, and when top management appearances are needed. A typical SMT can cover 12 to 20 stations in a few hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for cable/satellite proliferation and time-shifted viewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Cable and satellite have multiplied channel choices and extended viewing via on-demand services and digital recorders, changing viewing patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers and communicators must recognize that viewers use DVRs and on-demand options; programming and placement strategies should account for fragmented, time-shifted audiences and interactive cable services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize new media's four core challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: The new media environment poses at least four challenges for public relations practitioners: (1) staying abreast of changing technology, (2) responding to the demand for transparency, (3) dealing with new media players who communicate directly with stakeholders, and (4) representing organizations in the social media environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These imperatives should shape organizational strategy, staffing, monitoring, and crisis preparedness in a digitally networked environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay current with digital and social media technology and skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must adapt to rapid technological change and increasingly seek social media expertise when hiring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations need 24-hour monitoring, people who can move quickly and analyze results, and staff with skills to manage social platforms and real-time responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search engine optimization (SEO) for findability
rubrics_metrics.description: SEO aims to get an organization’s name to appear at or near the top of search results for relevant queries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search engines drive a large share of Internet traffic (study cited: 84% of users rely on search), and search ranking is based on relevance and importance. Incorporate SEO into online communications to increase visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constantly monitor the digital media environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Because information—true or false—spreads rapidly online, practitioners must be vigilant in scanning and monitoring digital media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard practices such as reading morning papers are insufficient; organizations need tools and processes to detect and respond to emerging issues, 'rogue opinions,' and viral conversations in real time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed, agility, and humility in social media response
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media demands fast, sensitive responses; organizations may have only hours or minutes to react to crises or negative publicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have a social media protocol and crisis communication plan; responses should be timely while maintaining appropriate tone, accuracy, and alignment with organizational principles. Case studies (Motrin, Cooks Source) illustrate damage from slow, insensitive, or combative responses; apologetic and humble responses help mitigate backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency as a mandatory organizational principle
rubrics_metrics.description: New media raise transparency to a new level: organizations cannot assume they can hide mistakes or control all information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Internet enables rapid sharing and amplification of information; failure to disclose in social campaigns or to be transparent damages relationships and organizational credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate and integrate communication functions (single voice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media convergence requires that internal and external communication programs use the same message strategy and be coordinated across organizational silos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies often centralize communications under one senior executive to ensure a single voice, which is especially important in crises to avoid mixed messages (analogy: the President has a press secretary rather than many spokespeople).

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with nontraditional gatekeepers (bloggers) while recognizing differing expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must work with bloggers and other new media influencers who act as gatekeepers but often demand higher transparency and access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bloggers may be credentialed alongside traditional media and can reach targeted, plugged-in audiences. However, the relationship is tenuous because bloggers typically expect more access and transparency than traditional media; monitor the blogosphere and use blogs as part of a web-savvy outreach strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and plan for citizen journalism and user-generated content
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone with a camera phone can report news; citizen journalists and social platforms often break news faster than traditional outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Twitter reports during crises (Mumbai attacks, Hudson River landing). Public relations strategies should incorporate user-generated content monitoring and responses, and consider how to verify and integrate such material.
